analysis.one_liner: Bans ICE from signing private detention contracts that guarantee minimum numbers of immigrant detention beds.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: referred to the House Judiciary Committee on June 17, 2015 and to its immigration subcommittee on July 1, 2015, it died without any further action when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Private companies run many immigration detention facilities under contracts with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Some of those contracts include "guaranteed minimum" clauses that require taxpayers to pay for a set number of detention beds at a specific facility whether or not they are needed. This bill would bar ICE from negotiating any new contract, extension, or renegotiation that contains such a bed quota. It was introduced by Representative Ted Deutch and nine Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would no longer be billed for guaranteed minimums at private detention facilities; immigrants facing detention, since facilities would no longer have contractual pressure to keep occupancy up; and communities near detention facilities, which would not be locked into hosting a fixed detention population.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits ICE from negotiating any contract with a private detention company that contains a provision guaranteeing a minimum number of immigration detention beds at a specific facility [S2][S3].

The prohibition also applies to contract extensions and renegotiations, and takes effect for any negotiation beginning after enactment, so companies could not preserve quotas by simply renewing old deals [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to protect taxpayers and communities, since quota clauses commit public money to a fixed detention level regardless of actual need [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private detention companies, which would lose the guaranteed revenue streams that quota clauses provide, and would bear more risk if fewer detainees actually occupy their facilities.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it only bars quota provisions in negotiations that begin after enactment, so existing contracts with quotas would remain in force until they come up for extension or renegotiation [S3].

A good-faith objection is that guaranteed minimums give facilities predictable revenue, which private operators argue helps them keep facilities open and per-bed costs down; removing quotas shifts occupancy risk onto the companies, who may raise prices or close facilities, and could push ICE toward building more government-run detention space.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is concrete: quota clauses commit taxpayers to pay for detention capacity whether or not it is used, and this bill would stop new deals from including them. The cost falls on a small set of private detention companies that would lose guaranteed income, and the main weakness of the bill is that it does not reach existing contracts until they are renegotiated. On balance it is a modest, well-targeted taxpayer protection that died without ever being tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its immigration subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Representative Ted Deutch of Florida introduced the bill on June 17, 2015, joined by Representatives Bill Foster and Adam Smith as original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and on July 1, 2015 referred it to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Border Security [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].
All nine cosponsors were House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private detention companies are better off: the quota clauses that guarantee them payment for a minimum number of detention beds, including for beds that sit empty, remained in place because the bill never advanced. Taxpayers continue to fund those guaranteed minimums.

for.name: Rep. Ted Deutch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar ICE contracts containing guaranteed minimum detention bed quotas.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Border Security and never scheduled it for a hearing or committee vote in the eighteen months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No one voted on the bill, so no opposition votes exist; sponsorship was entirely Democratic, with all nine cosponsors being House Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar quota clauses in new and renegotiated ICE contracts, ending guaranteed minimum bed payments that keep public money flowing to these companies regardless of how many beds are actually filled. Their interest in keeping quotas runs against both taxpayers, who pay for unused beds, and detainees, since guaranteed occupancy gives facilities a contractual stake in detaining more people.
